questions.question_text: Which statement best defines a **random variable**?

options.text: A variable whose numerical values are determined by the outcomes of a random process.
A variable that is chosen haphazardly without any defined sample space.
options.why: Confuses a mathematical random variable with arbitrary choice.

options.text: Any qualitative description of an experimental outcome, such as colour or flavour.
options.why: Random variables must produce numerical values, not qualitative descriptors.

options.text: A fixed constant value that does not change between repeated trials.
options.why: A random variable takes varying outcomes across trials, not a fixed constant.

questions.solution_text:
A random variable assigns a numerical value to each outcome of a random process.
A variable whose numerical values are determined by the outcomes of a random process.

questions.question_text:
A meteorologist measures the total daily sunshine duration in hours at an airport.
Why is this variable classified as continuous?

options.text: Because time is measured on a continuous scale and can take any real value in $[0, 24]$.
Because sunshine either occurs or does not occur, giving two separate states.
options.why: Treats the duration of sunshine as a binary event rather than a measurable quantity.

options.text: Because time is always recorded in whole hours on official weather charts.
options.why: Confuses the precision of the recording format with the nature of the physical variable.

options.text: Because the number of sunshine hours must always be a positive integer.
options.why: Sunshine duration can be fractional (e.g. $6.35$ hours), not just whole integers.

questions.solution_text:
Sunshine duration is a measured time quantity that can take any value in the interval $[0, 24]$ hours.
Because time is measured on a continuous scale and can take any real value in $[0, 24]$.

questions.question_text:
A card is drawn from a standard deck of $52$ cards $4$ times with replacement.
Let $X$ be the number of Kings drawn.
What is the set of all possible values of $X$?

options.why: Omits the outcome where zero Kings are drawn in all $4$ trials.
Uses the total deck size instead of the number of cards drawn in the experiment.
Confuses the total number of Kings in the deck with the possible outcomes of the sample.

questions.solution_text:
In $4$ draws with replacement, the number of Kings can be $0, 1, 2, 3$, or $4$.
$X \in \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}$

questions.question_text: Which of the following random variables is **continuous**?

options.text: The volume of petrol in litres dispensed into a car fuel tank.
The number of petrol stations in a metropolitan suburb.
options.why: The count of petrol stations is a discrete whole number.

options.text: The number of customer transactions at a service station in an hour.
options.why: The count of transactions is a discrete integer.

options.text: The price per litre displayed in whole cents on the price board.
options.why: A price board in whole cents takes discrete stepped numerical values.

questions.solution_text:
Volume is a measurable physical quantity that can take any real value in an interval.
The volume of petrol in litres dispensed into a car fuel tank.

questions.question_text:
A digital bathroom scale records a person's mass to the nearest $0.5\text{ kg}$.
Why is body mass classified as a continuous random variable?

options.text: Because actual body mass can take any real value on a continuous interval; the $0.5\text{ kg}$ steps reflect scale precision only.
Because the scale displays values with fractional parts like $.5$.
options.why: Having fractional values like $0.5$ does not make a variable continuous if steps are fixed.

options.text: Because body mass changes randomly every single second of the day.
options.why: Random fluctuations over time do not define the continuous nature of a variable.

options.text: Because body mass is a discrete variable that has been converted into a continuous variable by the scale.
options.why: Body mass is inherently continuous; the scale discretises it, not the reverse.

questions.solution_text:
Mass is inherently continuous; the instrument's display resolution does not alter the underlying variable.
Because actual body mass can take any real value on a continuous interval; the $0.5\text{ kg}$ steps reflect scale precision only.

questions.question_text:
Two standard six-sided dice are rolled.
Let $D$ be the absolute difference between the two numbers rolled ($D = |\text{Die 1} - \text{Die 2}|$).
What is the set of possible values of $D$?

options.why: Omits $0$ (when both dice show the same number) and incorrectly includes $6$.
Includes negative values when the variable is defined as an absolute difference.
Omits $0$, which occurs whenever both dice roll the same value.

questions.solution_text:
Minimum difference is $|1 - 1| = 0$.
Maximum difference is $|6 - 1| = 5$.
$D \in \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$

questions.question_text:
Which pair correctly identifies the classification of both random variables?
$X$: The number of phone calls received by a helpline between 9:00 am and 10:00 am.
$Y$: The duration (in minutes) of a randomly selected phone call.

options.text: $X$ is discrete (counted calls) and $Y$ is continuous (measured duration).
$X$ is continuous and $Y$ is discrete.
options.why: Reverses the classification of both random variables.

options.text: Both $X$ and $Y$ are discrete variables.
options.why: Incorrectly classifies call duration as discrete rather than measurable time.

options.text: Both $X$ and $Y$ are continuous variables.
options.why: Incorrectly classifies the count of telephone calls as continuous.

questions.solution_text:
$X$ is a count of calls (discrete), while $Y$ is a continuous measurement of time.
$X$ is discrete (counted calls) and $Y$ is continuous (measured duration).

questions.question_text:
Let $X$ be the continuous random variable representing the lifetime (in hours) of an electronic component.
Which statement is mathematically true for $X$?

options.text: $P(X = 1000) = 0$, but $P(999.5 \le X \le 1000.5) > 0$ for a non-zero probability density.
$P(X = 1000) > 0$ because $1000$ hours is a specific possible lifespan of the component.
options.why: For a continuous variable, the exact point probability is always $0$.
Assumes single points have positive probability in continuous distributions.

options.text: $P(X = 1000) = 1$ if the manufacturer guarantees the component lasts $1000$ hours.
options.why: A guarantee does not make a single continuous point have probability $1$.

questions.solution_text:
Continuous variables have $P(X = c) = 0$ for every single value $c$.
$P(X = 1000) = 0$, but $P(999.5 \le X \le 1000.5) > 0$ for a non-zero probability density.
